Mr. Speaker, let's get back to the point. We are talking about the responsibility of the Minister of State (Finance) and her colleague the Minister of Finance for the banking system, and in particular in this case the fact that the Northland Bank has been hung on the peg and is still left dangling day after day with no resolution. We have to ask ourselves why.
The first reason, Mr. Speaker, is the incredible state of the illusion that exists in the Progressive Conservative Government as to what the problem is. We saw it tonight in the incredible performance of the Associate Minister of Defence (Mr. Andre). I was reminded, listening to him speak, of a news item I reads in a magazine a couple of weeks back about a new defence acquisition by the United States called the "Sergeant York gun," a weapon on which they spent about $1.5 billion. After all that investment of time and money it was found that it made a lot of noise but did not function.
Well, Mr. Speaker, we have our own "Sergeant York gun" right here in the House of Commons in the person of the associate Minister of Defence. Our new acquisition! We didn't invest $1 billion in him. One couldn't even begin to get that price. One couldn'teven get $ 1 for him. But he certainly is the Canadian equivalent of a "Sergeant York gun": a lot of noise, a big bang-but it doesn't work. It can't hit the target; it has no ammunition. The Secretary of State of the United States junked the Sergeant York gun and I suspect, from what we have seen in the last several days, that it will soon be the turn of the Associate Minister of National Defence to be junked by his Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), just like he is junking everyone else as he proceeds down the pathway of glory. He used the argument that somehow, in the convoluted sense of logic across the way, everything was a result of the National Energy Program, that the real cause was the NEP. That is fantasyland. I do not ask you, Mr. Speaker, to take my word for it. You should take the word of the Minister of State for Finance. What did she say in her September 2 statement as to why they had to take action against the Canadian Commercial Bank and Northland? It was because of the bad U.S. loans they had made and because of the bad management of those loans. It had nothing to do with the nonsense and fiction which we are hearing from other Hon. Members. At least the Minister of State for Finance, probably reading from a press

September 25, 1985
release of her officials, got that one straight. There were $300 million, or whatever is the figure, of bad loans in energy development in southern California and in bad real estate speculation on the West Coast. They were a large part of the problems of those western banks.
Hon. Members opposite became involved in a debate about the NEP. Obviously I am a great servant of the Speaker of the House and would not want to deviate from the rules.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 31 FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY OF NORTHLAND BANK
speechtext:
I know the Hon. Member opposite does not read much, so I will draw to his attention something which came out on the wire today concerning the great energy policies of his own Government. A Canadian Press report today indicated how the Conservative Government, this so-called great Government based upon wise business experience, has just lost another $1 billion of taxpayers' money by making a ruling on the Gulf take-over which allowed the particular company involved to find a loophole in the tax system so that it would not have to pay $1 billion in taxes on that particular energy deal. Let us see all those Members rising in their places and cheering, as they did five times during Question Period, for that particular piece of brilliance on the part of their Government in its energy policy. It only lost $1 billion on the banks and another $1 billion this week on the Gulf take-over! We are reaching the point where "what's a billion" is the label of this Government. It just does not care. It does not even understand it any more. The fact of the matter is that that financial institution overextended its capacity and, when it came time to make a judgment on what to do about it, the problems began. In that event a Minister of the Crown must be held accountable.
Let us look at the record of what took place. The auditors for Canadian Commercial Bank were not even asked for their opinion on that weekend. In a statement before the Finance Committee, representatives of Clarkson Gordon, the auditors, said that they were not even asked for their advice. These were the people who were looking after the financial affairs. The bankers who were invited to come in-and they said so in very clear terms-had their own misgivings. The Royal inspection team which was asked to inspect it indicated that it made no recommendation because it could not uncover enough information. Also, according to the CP story, the fact that the bankers could not do a detailed analysis of the Commercial's books was making them nervous during the meetings that weekend. One banker complained that when additional information was requested, the Government handed out the same quarterly statements which were given to shareholders. A decision of incredible and major proportions was being made by the Government and the people who were asked to investigate could not get the information they requested. Then, these so-called brave guardians of the new economic order, the Minister of State for Finance and the Minister of Finance, were not even at the meetings. They could not be bothered. I suppose there was a party down in the annex which they had to
attend. They could not get around to going to the meetings when $1 billion was at stake. The Minister of State for Finance said: "That is not my responsibility; it is that of the officials".
Just this week a Minister resigned because he overruled his officials and stepped in on the tuna fish case. Now we have the Minister of State for Finance saying that it is only $1 billion and that it is only the first failure of a bank since 1923. She had something else to do that weekend and could not be bothered to attend. The Minister of Finance, the Minister who is ultimately accountable, could not be found either. Is that ministerial accountability?
They want to know why Canadians were worried and were asking who was in charge, when the two accountable Ministers were nowhere to be found on a weekend when $1 billion was going down the drain. Perhaps we should ask where the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) was at the time of the Gulf deal. We know that she was on an island somewhere in the Straits of Georgia. She was not around when these rulings were made, either. Yet, they want to know why Canadians are concerned and why we are having an emergency debate. The fact of the matter is that that serious misstep, that incredible lack of accountability displayed by the Ministers of the Government on that March weekend, set in motion the sequence of events which is now putting the Northland Bank in jeopardy. It is an incredible fallacy for the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and other Ministers to rise and say that they are defending western Canada. They are the ones who started to put the Northland Bank down the drain on March 22. Rather than taking the action they should have taken on that weekend, they began to pull the plug. As the officials of that bank said, they were going through their own rescue operations beginning in the summer. At the very time when they were getting their line of credit reduced down to zero and beginning to reorganize their portfolio, the Government stepped in on the September weekend, tied the two banks together and said that Northland was in the same predicament as CCB. Suddenly they want to know why people get nervous and start pulling out their deposits and why Northland is in trouble. Is this the saviour of western Canada? Is this a Government which stands up for the West? It had the opportunity to provide major support for at least one of those institutions and, instead, we will lose both of them. That is the simple equation, that is the simple result. Because of a serious lack of judgment and a serious lack of responsibility on the part of the two Ministers responsible for our financial arrangements, we are not only in the position of losing one major financial institution in the west; we are in danger of losing both.
As one of my colleagues said earlier in the debate, the reason for this emergency debate is to say that we still do not believe that it has to happen. We still believe that Northland might be saved, if only the Government would start exercising its responsibility, acting like a Government and making decisions, rather than dodging, weaving, defending, protesting and misinterpreting day after day in the House of Commons. We
September 25, 1985

have heard the Minister of State for Finance and the Minister of Finance plead: "Oh, if you only understood" and say that if the Opposition acted as their spiritual counsellor, everythig would be all right. We ask them to stand up and act like Ministers. We ask them to do their duty and to live up to their responsibilities. They are not doing these things. As each day goes by, the situation becomes more perilous and the future of Northland Bank looks more dim. That is why this emergency debate was called. I pay my respects to the members of the New Democratic Party for putting forward the motion against the opposition of the Government.
I know that I am not supposed to say that there is a distinct lack of ministerial representation in the House. We are talking about hundreds of millions of dollars of Canadian money in the bank and about a potential $500 million bail-out. Mr. Speaker, look at how much care and concern there is on the part of Members of the Government, especially the Ministers responsible. Ask yourself whether that is the way to behave. Is that the way the Government will win plaudits, justify its mandate and go on to the new millennium which has been promised? It is hardly likely. I know that it has been a tough day, a tough week, a tough month and a tough year for Government Members. It is going to get a lot tougher because the track record up to now simply shows that they are becoming confused and immobilized, and there is a wonderful word "immobiliser" that was attached to all the French Governments during the 1950s and 1960s. It described a state of mind of members of the Government at that time in the French Fourth Republic which was an incapacity, an inability to decide, to know what they wanted to do, to give direction. That is the problem that we see prevalent. That is the disease that is spreading day by day on the government side of this House.
We can go to the sources. I do not necessarily want to start saying who is to blame although in our system there is only one person to blame and that is the person who forms the Government, sets the tone, sets the framework. What we are seeing in this financial institution is that very same state of paralysis. My colleague tonight laid out some steps that should be taken to come to grips with the Northland situation, to try to deal with that bank's problems and responding to them. Instead we have, in hockey terms, a team that only knows how to play defence and doesn't know how to shoot the puck any more, it doesn't know to go on offence. It simply does not any longer know how to mount a well co-ordinated attack upon a problem.
I stand here as a westerner who has managed to survive there. I fully agree, a mandate was given, but mandates can be burned out. I only remind the House of the wonderful mandate that was given to the Diefenbaker Government back in 19571958. They burned that out in four years and wore out their welcome very quickly for exactly the same reason, confusion, indecision and lack of direction. If there is any lesson in history it should be that lesson how a strong mandate given by the Canadian people was frittered and flustered away by a
Government that did not know what it wanted to do or how to get there.
History is repeating itself day by day. That is what we are seeing taking place. The tragedy is that a lot more was expected. There was a lot more benefit of doubt being offered and it is still there but the fact of the matter is that it is not being earned.
I believe that if the Minister of State for Finance could somehow forget the posturing, get away from the excuses, get away from trying to defend what is indefensible and begin zeroing in on the problem we could still have a Northland Bank working in western Canada, as a viable institution, but I do not think there is much time left for her and her colleague, the Minister of Finance to take that action.
If there is any message that should come out of this debate tonight it is that the clock is ticking, the time is short and a lot of Canadians are looking to them for some decisions very soon.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 31 FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY OF NORTHLAND BANK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we called for this emergency debate because we are not satisfied that the Government is prepared to give all the information which is required by the people of Canada through their Members of Parliament who represent them, to know what ought to be done with the Northland Bank. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, we have every reason, based on past experience, to believe that not only is the Government not prepared to give us all the information but the fact is that the Government does not have all of the information. I say that because when we ask questions about the Northland Bank we are not talking about one isolated case of a financial institution which is in trouble. We have had a whole series first of financial institutions and trust companies and now banks which are in trouble.
How did the Minister try to deal with our criticisms, with the questions we asked tonight? She had two arguments. First of all, she blamed the difficulties of the financial institutions on the former Government. She said quite properly and correctly that the former Government had not passed the necessary legislation, did not have the adequate monitoring or supervisory system to deal with the kinds of problems that have arisen in recent years.
She was correct, and for that the former Liberal Government needs to be criticized in the strongest terms. But we have had three very serious financial situations, two failures and one probable failure, the one we are discussing tonight, since this Government took office. We had the Pioneer Trust problem; we had the Canadian Commercial Bank problem and now we are dealing with the Northland. When this Government took office it knew that there were tremendous problems. We have been accused by members on the Government side of using scare tactics. We have been told that we do not know anything about business. It is as if, Mr. Speaker, because we are frequently critical of the way the so-called free enterprise system works that therefore we cannot contribute anything useful.
We are not the only ones saying these things. A recent issue of The Globe and Mail "Report On Business" lists 17 finan-

September 25, 1985
cial institutions, trust companies and banks, which have gone sour, which in fact have gone bankrupt since 1980. According to Arthur Johnson who started one of these articles in this "Report On Business", the headline on his story is "A Billion-Dollar Bailout":
Belying its pinstripe image. Canada's bank, trust and loan industry is in a mess. The cost of cleaning things up: $1.2 billion of public money.
Mr. Speaker, I believe Arthur Johnson underestimated the cost because what he did not include there was the money which the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation is going to have to put in. I understand that they will be required to put in $1.5 billion and that they have more than $1 billion in property which they took over as a result of the collapse of the Rosenberg trust company. That money which the CDIC will be putting in comes through premiums paid by the banks but we ought to be under no illusions, the premiums paid by the banks have become part of the cost of the banks' operation and will be paid for by the banks' customers, by the people of Canada, so we are talking about billions of dollars of public money.
I say, Mr. Speaker, yes, the seeds of the difficulties were created by the failure of the former Liberal Government to put into place the kinds of laws and the kind of monitoring and regulatory system that would have obviated the difficulties, but this Government had enough time to learn the facts of life so that we should not be in the situation which we are at the present time with the Northland Bank.
I was asked by my colleagues to be a member of the finance committee last May and June when we were looking at the Canadian Commercial Bank. The committee held a great many meetings. We heard evidence from officials of the banks, from the Inspector General, from the Governor of the Bank of Canada and from representatives of two of the largest auditing firms in this country. We heard one story of disaster after another. We heard one story of misrepresentation and failure to act after another. When it was all over, the Government did not listen to the evidence or realize that the system was not working. It did not realize that the Inspector General had neither the ability nor the desire to do the job he should have been doing and that the Governor of the Bank of Canada vouched for the Canadian Commercial Bank without any information at all. After all the evidence had been given, he still maintained that in his view the officers of that bank were still capable of managing the bank.
At that time, we said that the Inspector General of Banks had been derelict in his duties. At that time, we said that the Governor of the Bank had vouched for the bank without having any knowledge on which to base that kind of statement. We did not have all the evidence before us and as has already been pointed out by some of my colleagues, the Inspector General, who we thought worked for the Government and people of Canada although his salary is paid by the banks, refused to give us this very important evidence that was required.
Did the Inspector General learn of the difficulties of the Canadian Commercial Bank only a few weeks before the crisis came up? I say that if he did, he is totally incompetent. About two years before the bank got into the difficulties which became known by everyone, the Superintendent of Insurance became aware that Leonard Rosenberg of whom we now know a great deal had become involved with the Canadian Commercial Bank. The Superintendent became aware that either he himself or other members of his family had control not of 10 per cent of the bank's shares, the limit permitted by the Bank Act, but that he controlled more than 20 per cent of the shares. He became aware as well that Mr. Rosenberg was involved in some very fancy financial deals with the then President of the Canadian Commercial Bank, Mr. Eaton.
We never learned whether or not the Superintendent of Insurance contacted the Inspector General of Banks to tell him about these things. Surely that was the point at which the Inspector General should have known that he ought to keep a very close eye on the operations of the Canadian Commercial Bank. However, he did not do so.
There was another point at which the Inspector General would have heard a warning bell if he were listening. That was when the regulatory agency in the United States which monitors bank operations took a look at the Westland Bank which was 100 per cent owned by the Canadian Commercial Bank. At that time, the regulatory agency in the United States put the Westland Bank on notice that it was operating contrary to the rules and regulations of the policies of the American banking system. What happened then? The Directors of the Canadian Commercial Bank proceeded to buy, rather than a minority part of the Westland Bank, 100 per cent of it.

speechtext: Order, please. I would like to know when the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) will deal with the Northland Bank. He has a few minutes left. I hate to call anyone to order on relevancy and particularly a senior Member of the House. However, I would hope that he would deal with the Northland Bank.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 31 FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY OF NORTHLAND BANK
speechtext:
As I indicated at the beginning of my speech, Mr. Speaker, we are not merely dealing with the Northland Bank. Unfortunately, this is not an isolated case. It is one more illustration of the failure of our system to see that these kinds of things do not happen.
I cannot deal in detail with the Northland Bank as I can with the Canadian Commercial Bank because we have not yet held hearings. We do not know about all the things which happened at the Northland Bank. However, we do know some of what happened at the Canadian Commercial Bank. I am saying that the Government should have learned a lesson and it did not. That is the point which I am trying to make.
The Inspector General was derelict in his duties. If he did not have the staff or the authority-both of which are possible-then he could have come to Parliament to say that he could not do his job because he did not have the staff or authority and I would not have been critical of the Inspector General. However, he did not do any of those things.
September 25, 1985

Let us take a look at the Governor of the Bank of Canada. When the financial sections of newspapers began to report that there was trouble at the Canadian Commercial Bank, the Governor of the Bank of Canada did something which was unprecedented. One evening he called The Globe and Mail to say that he vouched for the Canadian Commercial Bank as a viable operation. How could the Governor of the Bank of Canada have said that? That was when the Canadian Commercial Bank was in trouble.
A couple of days ago, the Governor of the Bank of Canada made a speech in Toronto. Let me read part of what the Governor of the Bank of Canada said as reported by The Globe and Mail of September 25, 1985:
"The Bank of Canada," ... "is not involved in monitoring the financial soundness of individual banks and supervising their behaviour. Parliament has not given us that responsibility or the powers that would enable us to fulfil that function. The Bank of Canada has no bank auditors, no bank examiners, no power to require details of individual loans, deposits or any other kind of private transaction."
The Governor of the Bank of Canada has condemned himself with his own words. If that is true, and of course it is true, then the Governor of the Bank of Canada had no business vouching for the Canadian Commercial Bank. Not only did he vouch for the Canadian Commercial Bank before it became obvious that its survival was very unlikely but he came before the committee of which I was a member in June after we heard evidence from the bank officials, the Inspector General and the auditors to say that he still had confidence that the officers of the bank could do an adequate job. The mistake this Government made was to take the advice of the Inspector General of Banks and the Governor of the Bank of Canada.
I wish to say something about the auditors as well. I hope that the organization of auditors will take a serious look at what happened at the Canadian Commercial Bank and at the responsibility of the auditors, not just to their customers who pay their auditing accounts, but to the people of Canada. What did these auditors do? They reported to the directors of the bank that the bank had serious problems. They did that, I presume, after a fairly careful examination of the bank's business operation. However, that was in a report given to the directors of the bank, a report which was never made public. What they provided to the bank was a statement which was made public that the bank was a viable operation. I say there is something seriously wrong with a situation in which auditors would carry out that type of action. They helped in misleading the people of Canada. They put the depositors in great trouble.
I would like to conclude my remarks by saying to the Minister, and to the Government, that we accept her criticisms of the former Government. We accept her promises that there will be better regulations in upcoming legislation. If we had not looked at the record of this Government since it took office and how it has failed to look at the realities of the situation, and how it has failed to take the advice of the top officers in
Government service, we would have reason to believe that something better would come about in the future. When the Minister promises she will encourage more companies to get into the financial services field and when she promises more competition, I ask: How many regulators? How many monitors will we have? What more competition will mean is more failures and hundreds of millions of dollars more down the drain.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 31 FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY OF NORTHLAND BANK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for all Hon. Members to have to sit in the House at 11.30 p.m. is a sign that the situation is very serious, that hardly one year after assuming power, this Government, which had been in the Opposition for sixteen years and which, during the last election campaign, had promised the moon to the Canadian people claiming that it would know what to do once in power, Mr. Speaker, we have reached the point where, because of incompetence-

Mr. Speaker, the mistake was made when the Government did not come clean and failed to tell everything it knew; things simply got worse when this inept and incompetent Government decided to go ahead without even knowing whether those two banking institutions would be able to pull through. We Quebecers know all about such shenanigans, Mr. Speaker. They did not simply appropriate the taxpayer's money without having a clear financial picture of the situation. That is what I call responsible people.
Mr. Speaker, I am not afraid to say that it was a party I fought against, the Parti quebecois. However, I tip my hat to them because they have shown what they could do. Now, without knowing what is going on, the Federal Government decides to come in and organize a bail-out by using the taxpayers' money. Mr. Speaker, we have to say who will pay for all this. speechtext:
As they always are, correct.
One of the sacred cows in our society is, of course, the banking system. In fact, we were told that banks never go bankrupt because we Canadians have done it better than the Americans have done it. We have a Bank Act and we have not had a bank go belly-up for 62 years, until the Canadian Commercial Bank, of course, and the spin-off effect on the Northland Bank. Everyone has come to think of banks as pillars of strength in the economy. Somehow or other these
September 25, 1985

banks are the pillars of Canadian society. They are symbols of stability and continuity. Indeed, last spring I suggested that the Minister of State for Finance was launching a new bank when she came in here and said they were going to rescue this bank and restore the confidence of Canadians in the banking system. We will not let them down! She called on Members of Parliament to support her in this bail-out effort, this rescue attempt. But we on this side of the House recognized what was happening; that the Minister of State for Finance and the Minister of Finance were like the Captain on the deck of the Titanic rearranging the deck chairs as the ship was going down.
As we have witnessed over the last few weeks, this thing has become more an more curious. It has unfolded in strange and bewildering ways. Let us look at how this thing has happened. You have to imagine this. We have a Bank Act and an Inspector General of Banks. You do not get a title like a general unless you can give some orders. So they have nice titles such as the Inspector General of Banks. I will bet you always thought this chap investigated banks. I bet you think and the public always thought that the Inspector General had an army of inspectors; that they would march up to the great columns, to the very stability of the capitalists in this country, to the very halls, to their Valhallas and knock on their doors and say: We have come to inspect your bank!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 31 FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY OF NORTHLAND BANK
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 31 FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY OF NORTHLAND BANK
speechtext: I thought that. In my naivite I thought that was the way it worked.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 31 FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY OF NORTHLAND BANK
speechtext: A lot of people did.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 31 FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY OF NORTHLAND BANK
speechtext: But I found out since this episode that that ain't the way it is. It ain't the way it is!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 31 FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY OF NORTHLAND BANK

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 31 FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY OF NORTHLAND BANK

They will check everything and report back to head office that the branch is fine. Head office then sends this report to the Inspector General of Banks. One would think that he would send out his inspectors, but he only has seven inspectors. I always thought that the Inspector General was paid with taxpayers' money. I
thought that we allotted a sum of money to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to pay the Inspector General and his army of seven inspectors and 42 stenographers and filing clerks.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 31 FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY OF NORTHLAND BANK

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 31 FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY OF NORTHLAND BANK
speechtext:
Yes, that's it. You got it. Mr. Speaker, he's got it. In that way you can be assured that you are getting a real tough inspection. The poor chap does not know what the devil is happening in the branches. He is sequestered in the basement of the Bank of Canada building with a few pictures on the wall. He sits there stamping documents thinking he is working hard.
I thought that the Bank of Canada had a role to play in this. What role does the Governor of the Bank of Canada have? We all thought this guy spoke with some knowledge of what was going on in the bank, but he said:
The Bank of Canada is not involved in monitoring the financial soundness of individual banks and supervising their behaviour. Parliament has not given us that responsibility or the powers that would enable us to fulfil that function. The Bank of Canada has no bank auditors, no bank examiners, no power to require details of individual loans, deposits or any other kind of private transaction.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 31 FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY OF NORTHLAND BANK
speechtext: How does he know what's going on?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 31 FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY OF NORTHLAND BANK
speechtext: That is the thing, he doesn't know. The Minister of Finance and his sidekick, "Billion Dollar Barbara", are sitting over there and they have a problem. They wonder from whom they should seek advice. They ask advice of the Governor of the Bank who doesn't know a bloody thing about the loan. They also ask the Inspector General of Banks, the minion of the dominion banks. Can you imagine that, Mr. Speaker? That reminds me of the story of the fellow who brought an elephant to two blind fellows and asked if they could feel the animal and tell what it was. One of them felt it and said that he thought it was a camel because it had a hump. The other one said he thought it was a coyote, but they were both wrong. That is the same problem we have here.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 31 FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY OF NORTHLAND BANK
speechtext: Who is in charge?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 31 FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY OF NORTHLAND BANK
speechtext: Well, that is a good question. No one is in charge.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 31 FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY OF NORTHLAND BANK
speechtext: Who's supposed to be in charge?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 31 FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY OF NORTHLAND BANK
speechtext:
The Government has the responsibility.
There are no regulations enforcing how the banks operate. I want to put on record a case history of how they do operate.
1 received a letter from the firm of Pharand Kuyek, Barristers. That firm appeared for a poor fellow by the name of Robert Newcombe in a bankruptcy trial involving the Nation-

September 25, 1985
al Bank of Canada. I will read the relevant parts. This is a public document so I am not revealing anything that is secret. The letter reads in part:
I acted for Mr. Robert Newcombe who was involved in an action with Mr. Tom Leroy and Leroy Trucking Limited. Mr. Newcombe had gone to the bank, purchased trailers and financed those through the bank and entered into an oral agreement with Mr. Leroy to the effect that Mr. Leroy would make all bank payments, maintain the trailers and that those sums paid and the maintenance of the trailers would be equivalent of lease payments to Mr. Newcombe who was leasing the trailers to Mr. Leroy.
Of course, Leroy went belly-up and they came against Mr. Newcombe. The evidence disclosed that the bank loaned the sum of $60,000 to Tom Leroy and a second amount of $60,000 to Leroy Trucking Limited. They could not lend any further moneys to Mr. Leroy or his company because the supervisors in Toronto would learn that the second loan to the trucking company in the amount of $60,000 was contrary to the rules and regulations of the bank. That is why they set Mr. Newcombe up as the strawman in that loan. It was interesting when they go to the bankruptcy hearing and put one of the bank agents on the witness stand. The court transcript reads in part as follows:
Q. I see. So, what you're really saying is that you were working for the Bank and you were preparing false reports, is that what you're telling us?
A. Not on my own accord.
Q. But you were doing it?
A. Well, under supervision, yes.
Q. You were all doing it?
A. Yes.
Q. So the employees at the Bank were actually creating false reports, credit reports, so that people could borrow money?
And the answer, Mr. Speaker, was "yes". That is just one small example of how the regulations governing the Bank were never enforced. In the same way, the Canadian Commercial Bank made loans that were not secured and the regulations that should govern those transactions were never enforced.
It is not only this Government that is responsible for not putting the proper mechanisms in place to enable the banks to live up to the regulations Parliament set out in the Bank Act. The responsibility has to be shared by the previous governments which, from 1968 to 1984, with the exception of the nine-month Clark fiasco, were all Liberal. The previous Government must take responsibility for the fact that it never lived up to its responsibility to ensure that the proper procedures were put in place. With these two fiascos on the horizon the present Government is running for cover. It will not produce this document and that document and the big cover-up is on. It did not even want this debate to take place tonight. It wants the matter to go before a committee, but there is no point in having a parliamentary committee if the conclusions of the committee are already ordained. If the committee cannot have all the necessary documents, it obviously cannot come to any conclusions that would give confidence to the Canadian people again.
When the Minister brought forward the Bill to save the bank in the spring I remember telling her that she was launching a bank. We were told that everything would be fine
now and that they would never have to come back to Parliament again. Considering she was depending on Bouey XIV and the other fellow, the Inspector General of Banks for advice-two peas in a pod who knew as much about the banking system as the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall)-they blindly led the blind and all four fell into the pit. But to our surprise and yours certainly, a few months later we saw that this Government's great promises and the word of the Prime Minister and his Ministers were not worth more than the bank's own assets. We found out that this Government had miserably failed on the whole issue. In that sense, Mr. Speaker, at a time when money is so hard to earn, so hard to get by for Governments, so scarce, seeing that a Government which claims to save on expenses, which claims to be sparing of its money, can afford to spend $1 billion simply to save, first, the Prime Minister's ego, second, the Minister of Finance's ego, and third, the Minister of State for Finance's ego, to name but a few. Mr. Speaker, I took it upon myself to call friends of mine living in western Canada and enquired as to how much that institution was basic and important in the minds of our westerners.
Let me tell you about their experience, their experience as ordinary westerners. You know, Mr. Speaker, that if you were applying for a loan of less than $1 million and were told to get lost ... In this emergency debate we are talking about the competence of a Government which was elected just over a year ago today. Many Canadians may still be watching the debate tonight. It is surprising the number of people who watch us on television. Ever since we returned on September 9 they have been wondering what on earth is going on in Ottawa. First they hear about "Billion Dollar Barbara" and her blank

September 25, 1985
cheque to the banks. They wonder how on earth we can get out of such a mess. They know about the CCB perhaps vaguely, because of a bail-out which took place six months ago. They know that over Labour Day weekend the Government said there was another bank in which there were $470 million of uninsured deposits and that it would pay those off as well, to bring the total up to $1 billion. Then the Minister of State for Finance assured the House that we were not losing any money at all because they knew back in March that they would have to pay that much, or words to that effect. She turned around and said: "Of course I was acting on the best judgment I could act on". Also she repeatedly told the House that they were acting because the bankers told them that it was okay to act.
I took the opportunity to participate in the hearings before the Finance Committee. I listened to some of the bankers over the course of the last week and a half. They were quite consistent in saying that they felt that the CCB was a can of worms. If they had been asked back in the spring, I suspect they would have said the same thing about the Northland Bank. However, they were being asked then for a judgment on the Canadian Commercial Bank.
Let us face it, the CCB and the Northland Bank are inextricably intertwined and the money which we will have to pay for the two of them is inextricably intertwined as well. The bankers said that they only went in because they were told that the CCB was viable by the Inspector General of Banks and by the Government of the Bank of Canada. They went in, not because they were able to make an independent judgment, but because they were told to go in by the Government or perhaps by a Prime Minister determined to do something for western Canada.
The questions of competence which have arisen boggle the mind. Suppose, Mr. Speaker, that you had not been elected to the House of Commons. In fact, you were in business in Toronto before coming to Parliament. Suppose your business considered the take-over of a substantial operation, some business that was up for sale. Would you have put a downpayment on that particular concern and made an irrevocable commitment without looking at the books of that particular company? Would you have looked at its receivables, its credit rating, its accounting system, its management or at its track record over the course of the previous few years? The answer is that if you were a competent businessman, of course you would have done all those things. However, in the case of CCB, none of those things were done.

I accept your judgment, Mr. Speaker. Of course several officers were in the chair, and possibly there may have been some discrepancy there as well.
I have spoken to Canadians who wonder what has happened to $1 billion of their money, particularly at a time of deficits. They know that the Government is in serious financial difficulty and that that difficulty has been greatly worsened by actions over the last few weeks.
Over the course of the spring a run took place in which a great amount of liquidity was withdrawn from the Northland Bank as well as from the CCB. The money was taken from Northland Bank as a consequence of questions about the viability of two western banks, both of which shared a number of things in common. It is difficult to comment fully about the Northland Bank because that we do not have as much information as was made public about the CCB.
In commenting upon the Northland Bank and in calling for this emergency debate, we were moved to do so because of unprecedented actions last week. After being taken into trusteeship, and after the Government said that it would seek new management or some form of maintenance of the Northland Bank, the President of the Northland Bank-and that was approximately 18 days after it had been put into curatorship- said that contrary to the assurances of the Government on September 3, the Government appeared to be doing everything possible to put it under.
I should like to raise the following question of competence. If the Government was wrong about the one bank, then in fact it may well be wrong about the other. If the Government was wrong in failing to look at the assets of one bank, it seems to me that it may well have failed in looking at the assets of the other. If the Government was wrong because it failed to send in anyone to look at what was happening in the one bank where we had the details, it seems to me that it was wrong in failing to find out what the devil was happening with the Northland Bank. If the Government was wrong in saying that
September 25, 1985

the one bank was viable, as was said by the Minister of State for Finance, the Inspector General of Banks and the Governor of the Bank of Canada, one has to believe that it was wrong as well in stating that the Northland Bank was viable. If the Government was wrong in permitting or telling Mr. Bouey of the Bank of Canada to pour billions of dollars into the Canadian Commercial Bank, one has to say that it was likely wrong in putting large amounts of liquidity into the Northland Bank as well.
Now I admit that we are talking about far more questions than we are answers. We have heard repeatedly, as these two subjects, which are intertwined, have come up in the House over the course of the last couple of weeks, the Government say let us get it off to a committee and the committee can decide. I am sure there are some people watching this debate who have heard members of the Government say that and then suggest that it is our Party which has prevented this matter from going to committee.
I would point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that the Government has the carriage of the business of this House in their hands. They could very easily have brought forward their motion and simply pushed it through. They have the numbers to enable them to pass the motion if they had chosen to send the matter out to committee regardless of the fact that there was disagreement over the terms of reference to the particular committee.
I would point out as well, Mr. Speaker, that we in the New Democratic Party wanted to avoid having a committee that would simply serve as a whitewash for the waste of $1 billion of taxpayers' money on the Northland Bank and on the Canadian Commercial Bank. We felt that at the very least the people of Canada were entitled to some basic information and that we had to have some assurance that the committee could do an effective job.
We asked for the report that was prepared on the one bank that was investigated. We were not assured we could get it. We sought auditors' reports. We were told that they would be barred. We sought material from California. We were told that the Americans would not give it up. We sought the list of depositors who were going to be bailed out regardless of the fact that the depositors in the Northland Bank and the CCB were uninsured and had absolutely no legal claim on the Government of Canada or the Bank of Canada, and finally the Minister of State for Finance told us unequivocally in response to a question of mine the other day, "No, you will not have that information".
It was not just the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre speaking when I put that particular question; it was not just me as a spokesperson for my Party. I was speaking on behalf of taxpayers across Canada from Vancouver Island to St. John's who were saying, if we are going to spend $1 billion we want to know who is going to get that particular money. What I was hearing from the Minister of State for Finance was that not only was she refusing to make that list of depositors available
so that we could judge about the bank itself, so that people would know where the money was going, but I think the Government was going a step further.
I think that the Government is saying that when the Public Accounts come out in a year or two years time the whitewash job will have been applied to the statements about spending of the Government of Canada to the point where it will be impossible to know to whom payments have been made in the light of the failure of the Northland Bank and the Canadian Commercial Bank. The Government is so intent on protecting the interests of the financial community, the large investors and depositors who will stand to get the largest amount from this particular bail-out, they are prepared to distort the Public Accounts of Canada in order to keep that material away from the people of Canada, even though it is a year or two years hence.

They cannot claim irrelevantly, as one of the Ministers claimed in this debate, that it was the national energy policy that "made us do it".
I remember the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) making cracks about patronage and suggesting "It was the devil that made John Turner do it," and it was very funny during the course of the election campaign, Mr. Speaker. But a year after they took power, almost on the anniversary of September 4, 1984, Mr. Speaker, the new Government cannot claim that they were simply landed with a mess from the previous Government and that they can abdicate responsibility.
I commend the Minister of State for Finance for the coolness with which she has faced the situation, but I cannot commend her for the competence she has shown in this particular affair. She worked in the financial industry. She was a consultant and a former vice-president of an investment firm. She was in a position, as was the Minister of Finance who was in fact a president, I believe, of a financial firm on Bay Street, to know that no one loans money without first checking out the recipient. No one loans billions of dollars without looking at credit ratings, or buys a pig in a poke

without checking to see if the things that they have been told are true. We cannot allow ourselves to be stonewalled, Mr. Speaker, as has happened with the banks in question by managements which have proven themselves to be questionable, whose credibility is at stake and whose stewardship in terms of their responsibility to the public was seriously in question.

That is a Tory plot-a serious problem of contradictions, of absolute and incredible contradictions. If someone watched this debate or read the debates afterwards, they would see incredible contradictions, particularly if they knew what happened in the Standing Committees and in the House of Commons the last several weeks.
Members stand up here tonight in this debate and claim that the bankruptcies of the banks in western Canada were due to the Liberal policies of years ago. Then we had, as anybody knowledgeable on this subject would know, the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) stand in this chamber and say that the problems of these banks were created in recent months. In fact she even said to the Liberal Opposition "I have never said that the problens of the western banks were ever created by the national energy policy". Those are the exact words of the Minister of State for Finance. She went further and said in this chamber on March 29:
-how recently this had bubbled up from underneath.
Quoting figures from the United States she said:
-2,175 drilling rigs are operating in U.S., down 612 from December. .. 299 from last February.
The problem really came out of nowhere. ... how recently this had bubbled up from underneath.
Then we had the incredible statement by the Minister of State for Finance when she even said, as has been mentioned in this debate:
There are no other financial institutions in the country at the moment that are appearing to be insolvent in any way.
Then she went on to say "the bank is a solvent bank", referring to the CCB. She said "that the bank is not failing," and "could we please make that very clear. I find the vocabulary somewhat hysterical", and "this is not a failing bank". The Minister of State for Finance made those statements yet Conservative Members stand up in this chamber and claim
that the responsibility lies with the previous Government because of the national energy policy. We have the Minister of State for Finance contradicting that clearly. Even their own Minister contradicted what those Members have been saying. Even a Cabinet Minister from western Canada made a statement totally contradictory to what the Minister of State for Finance said.
The other main point that was missed must be put on the record. Here is a good question. Who was it who said, "We looked at a number of possibilities and we came up with what we felt was the most attractive solution for everyone. If a bank gets into trouble and gets merged into one of the "Big-Five" banks, we could end up with no regional banks. We indicated that we felt it was responsible for the Government to get involved."
Is this the Government of Canada not wanting a bank to merge with another bank when it was in trouble?
What happened with Northland? When the Bank of Canada cut off its deposits, the curator was brought in and the Minister of State for Finance said, "You go ahead and merge. We will even give you a bank that wants to merge with you". That particular bank did not know what she was talking about. It was a complete reversal of the policy stated by the Minister herself in this Chamber. It was the Minister of State for Finance who said the words to which I referred earlier. The contradictions are amazing. If I were outside of this Chamber, I could use another word which I am not allowed to use in the Chamber. It is absolutely incredible.
With what are we left? A Member of the New Democratic Party rose to make fun of the Inspector General of Banks. He said that the Inspector General of Banks is paid by the banks. That is not exactly correct, Mr. Speaker. The Inspector General of Banks is paid by the depositors to the extent of one-tenth of 1 per cent of depositors' money. That is the way it was until this Minister came along and tripled that amount. Why did she do that? Because the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation brought in about $37 million last year and about $125 million this year. The Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation is broke and owes over $1 billion. What does it have to do to fulfil the commitment in the legislation and pay the insured depositors? It has to borrow money. From where does it borrow that money? It borrows it from the Government of Canada. From where does the Government of Canada get the money? It borrows it and increases its own deficit. That is very interesting, Mr. Speaker.
That borrowed money covers the $420-million worth of insured depositors. From where does the money come for the $900-million worth of uninsured depositors? Does that come from the Government of Canada? Yes. Why does it come from the Government of Canada? Because this Government made an error. The Government made a moral and legal commitment to guarantee a return on the money of the depositors of that bank. It was a $900-million error.
September 25, 1985

Add that error to the money that has been borrowed to cover the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation funds, another $420 million. Let us not forget the $255 million used for this infamous bail-out which will supposedly be recovered on the sale of the assets for which the Government may only receive 50 cents on the dollar.
Who made the error? We can talk about the Inspector General of Banks who is indirectly paid by the banks through the depositors. Who is responsible for the state of Northland today? Who took this action? The banks said that they did not want to have anything to do with this. If they did want to have something to do with it, they should all be fired. What bank manager would give the ordinary man on the street $60 million with no evidence at all? However, that is what these bank executives did. Surely they had something upon which to base their decision.
Was it the Inspector General of Banks who made the error? No, because let us not forget that he was not allowed to look at the figures. He was allowed to look at an American report for a moment but he was not allowed to take a photocopy of it.
Was the error made by General Bouey, as some people refer to him? No, it was not his responsibility. He does not know anything about the banks. Who was at fault? Who was responsible for making this commitment? I will tell you who was responsible, Mr. Speaker. I am going to make a guess because nothing else makes sense.
On the one hand there is the Government of Alberta and on the other there is the Government of British Columbia which dealt with subordinate debentures. The Government of Canada shared equally with the Government of Alberta. Then the banks came in with money. Surely someone somewhere made the decision to put it all together. Who made that decision? The only conclusion to which I could come is that this happened as a result of a phone call from a provincial premier. Perhaps that is the answer. Perhaps a provincial premier, in this new spirit of federal co-operation, phoned the Government. It was not a premier from New Brunswick this time but probably the Premier of Alberta.
The taxpayers of Canada were committed to something through a political judgment which influenced the banks. Why else would the banks have loaned this money? The banks would only give the money if they got certain guarantees. They wanted to be able to write this money off on their bottom lines and they wanted to be recognized as depositors so that they would be covered if this thing did not work out. However, they really did not think that this was a good deal.
After all of this occurred, the Minister of State for Finance rose in the House to say the following, as reported on page 3518 of Hansard:
Mr. Chairman, I have tried to explain to the House that this solution was arrived at because, in the judgment of knowledgeable people-including the Governor of the Bank of Canada, a group of six chartered banks, the Inspector General and the Province of Alberta-the bank would have been a viable operation if the capital was provided to resolve its loan problems.
Who made the judgment relating to Northland? Again it must have been a political judgment. It was made because the
CCB bail-out did not work out. The Bank of Canada froze its assets as deposits. The curator went in and ordered that this bank would merge with that bank and that bank did not know what they were talking about. However, the Minister of State for Finance has made it pretty clear. She said that the previous judgment was made on the recommendation of the six banks, the Governor of the Bank of Canada and the Inspector General of Banks.
The evidence before the committee indicates that the banks say that they did not recommend this. The hon. gentleman who sits behind me has just said that someone is not telling the truth. As Hon. Members know, I cannot say that someone is not telling the truth here in this Chamber. In fact, I cannot even say it in such a way as to even suggest it. I wonder what the people of Canada are saying? We have heard nothing but absolute and total contradictions beyond any scope of the imagination. How can the Minister of State for Finance make a statement one day and then make a different statement the next? How can the bank make differing statements? How can the Inspector General of Banks make differing statements? Now, every single one of the presidents and chairmen of the boards of six banks are making statements contradicting each other. The conclusion one has to come to is that the aftermath of all this is an awfully big bill.
We now have two banks involved in similar situations. We have uninsured depositors being paid by a deposit insurance corporation which is almost broke. That corporation is borrowing from the Government of Canada to the tune of $1.4 billion. The Government is borrowing money when its policy is to not increase the deficit. Thus, our taxes have got to go up. Then there are the uninsured depositors. They are the ones who are being paid directly by the Government. Then there is the Government of Canada adding on to the deficit and having to borrow to make up the difference. It is pretty clear to an ordinary person like myself from Newfoundland that this is a bloody disaster. It is a scandal of the first order.

a rational person can come to the conclusions which these Ministers have come to-no one. It could not be concluded that it was the Inspector General of Banks who was definitely responsible. I will be brief, but if otherwise provoked, Mr. Speaker, I will deliver as violent and as partisan a speech as the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall). She did not address herself to the question. She only wanted to play politics. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that nothing would please me more, even at this late hour, to do the same.
The point I want to raise, Mr. Speaker, is of great concern to me as an Hon. Member who has been here for many years. We will come back to it because I know this is not the end. My concern is this new approach that the Government seems to be developing as it tries to say that we on this side, we in this Party, do not care about what is going on in western Canada. If that is to be the approach and the defence of the Government, it is an immense mistake as was so well described by my colleague, the Hon. Member from Newfoundland, who spoke prior to me. I think we will have to object. I think we will have to prolong the debate. I think we will have to ask for a new debate on the same issue.
It is my view, Mr. Speaker, and also those of us who read very attentively the mood of the country-which is well expressed by various editorialists from western Canada as well as from central Canada and the Maritimes-that the attitude that seems to be developing here will be very bad for the unity of this country. It is an attitude that the New Democratic Party or what is more important to us, the Official Opposition, which governed for so long-perhaps too long, and that is what Canadians decided-are not concerned about western Canada. The Canadian people decided to give the new Government a chance to show what it could do but if that new Government is going to pretend again and again, either directly or indirectly, that this debate, which was suggested by us, means that we do not care about western Canada, I believe we will play into the hands of those who believe in the division of this country. It is not healthy and I do not beg of my colleagues but I certainly urge my colleagues to tackle this very immense difficulty. We see the credibility of the banking system in this country being attacked and that is very serious.
I come from a province where the people are very conservative minded when it comes to the question of money. Many do not have the same faith in the banking system as some of my colleagues opposite. It is traditional. It is historical. It is well known that-

In French, we refer to this as la politique du bas de laine. [English]
They prefer to keep their money at home instead of putting it into the system. If there would be no more confidence in the banking system of our country, it would be disastrous economically for those who want to invest and for those who want to borrow money in order to create employment, because people will say, "We will invest somewhere else and not in Canada's banking system."
I was very saddened and upset and so were a lot of people when I, as well as the country as a whole, heard the Righ Hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) say, "This country
is bankrupt". Let us analyse this phrase, "the country is bankrupt". What is the meaning of that phrase outside of Canada? I just happen to have been to a banquet tonight given by Her Excellency the Governor General, for the President of Tanzania. I was asked by one of the guests who sat not far from me to try to explain to him what the effect on foreign aid would be if a country as wealthy as Canada, so well respected as Canada, so generous in external aid as Canada, was to be known as bankrupt. I must admit I forgot partisanship. When we talk to outsiders, we have to defend the country as a whole and not as a representative of a political Party. I had to agonize to find a good argument. I did not say the country was bankrupt. I was trying to explain that it is a phrase and did not mean exactly what it inferred.
For that person, however, it meant exactly that. For the people in my province it means it is a terrible situation, that the banking system does not work. If we are going to go on and on pretending that the banking system in this country is going down the drain, I can imagine where the people who have some wealth-I am not talking about those people who have $60, but those people who have more than $60,000-are going to recoup their money. I am in agreement with the President of the Bank who said, "Tough luck. If the workers of this country, the little people, through their tax, are going to bail out a lot of people, we want to know who is going to be bailed out. We want to know how much it will cost and what kind of money those people will receive". 1 am in agreement with that.
I could go on, as I said, Mr. Speaker. It was because of the tone of the Minister of State for Finance that I felt 1 must speak. The Minister made a very partisan speech and tried again to sneak into the debate the question that this Party does not care about the interests of western Canada. That is the reason I rose to speak tonight. I want to put on record that we in this Party try to the best of our ability to give fair treatment to all parts of this country. To try to make Canadians believe that we are debating the issue because we do not care for western Canada would only be divisive and anything which would be divisive is not good for the country. Therefore, I would like to bring to the attention of my colleagues who like to participate again and again in this debate not to use that kind of argument. If they were to do so-which is their right because, after all, we live in a democracy-I can assure them that in a much better prepared way, we would tackle any Hon. Member who would like to use that as an argument. I repeat, and I conclude, Mr. Speaker, that any Hon. Member who uses that kind of argument will find us standing and answering tit for tat any insinuation that we are going to divide this country, that we do not care for western Canada and that these people of this new Government care more than we do.
